flasher.title: Flash your ESP32-C5
flasher.intro: Choose a compiled .bin image from your computer, or use the bundled ESP32-C5 MicroPython image. The browser flashes the board directly over Web Serial.
flasher.imageHelp: For a merged image, use one .bin at 0x0. For separate bootloader, partition and app images, add each file with its build's own flash offset.
flasher.microPythonImageHelp: Flash the Pulsar C5 image at 0x0000; flash the Espressif generic or SparkFun image at 0x2000. For your own .bin, enter the offset from its build (not a standalone .app-bin).
flasher.sparkfunOnly: This option is for the SparkFun Thing Plus ESP32-C5 board. For Pulsar C5, select the Pulsar C5 or ESP32_GENERIC_C5 firmware.
flasher.offsetHelp: Use the offsets from your build output. Common ESP32-C5 offsets are bootloader 0x2000, partitions 0x8000 and app 0x10000, but your project may differ.
flasher.stepCable: Connect the board with a USB data cable and close any other serial monitor.
flasher.stepPort: Press Flash firmware and choose the board's serial port.
flasher.stepBoot: If connection fails, hold BOOT, press RESET, release RESET, then release BOOT and try again.
flasher.warning: Without a full erase, only the sectors covered by the images are erased. Other flash data remains. Do not unplug the board while writing.
flasher.eraseAllWarning: The entire flash will be erased, including saved .py scripts and board data. The selected firmware will then be written. Do not unplug the board during this process.
flasher.unsupported: This page needs HTTPS or localhost and a browser with Web Serial, such as Chrome or Edge on a desktop computer.
flasher.success: Firmware written. If the board remains in BOOT mode, press RESET to start it.
flasher.successManualReset: Firmware written. Press RESET on the board to start it.
flasher.logEmpty: The connection log will appear here.

hints.loudness: Speak or clap near the microphone. RMS is the average level; peak shows the loudest instant.
hints.clap: Adjust sensitivity until claps cross the threshold. The switch is virtual.
hints.recorder: Press Record, speak for two seconds, then press Play. The clip stays in the board's memory.
hints.spectrum: Hum and whistle to see which bands respond. These are eight test frequencies, not a full FFT.
hints.game: Choose a difficulty and press Start. Clap when GO appears; the cue sound comes from your browser.
hints.voice_fx: Record a take and try several effects with echo and filters. Processing happens after capture through the codec speaker.

p4Sensors.title: P4 on-board sensors
p4Sensors.sceneLabel: A 3D drone flown by the five on-board sensors
p4Sensors.sceneFallback: The five sensor readings remain visible.
p4Sensors.sceneLegend: Pressure lifts the drone · the magnetic field turns it · light moves the sun and switches the headlights · a near hand turns the radar red · the battery lights the LEDs · humidity thickens the clouds
p4Sensors.batteryNote: The battery gauge reads {{gauge}} %. The MAX17048 goes above 100 % when no LiPo is connected (it measures the charger) or before it has learnt a newly connected cell, so the charge shown comes from the cell voltage. The stream script restarts the gauge's estimate when it starts.

i2sAudio.title: Listen to I²S microphone
i2sAudio.intro: Install the included Pulsar C5 MicroPython firmware at 0x0000, run the I²S audio example for your wiring, then press Listen. PCM audio arrives over USB Serial/JTAG and plays on this page.
i2sAudio.gainNote: Only boosts playback in this browser. Lower the gain if it distorts; dBFS shows the original signal.
i2sAudio.gapBreakdown: Invalid PCM packets: {{packets}} · Playback buffer resets: {{playback}}
i2sAudio.gapNote: Do not use the microSD card while listening to I²S: both share GPIO27/7/26, and card activity can cause clicks. If Audio gaps still increases, check the USB cable and close other serial monitors. Gain changes volume only.
i2sAudio.signalNote: Signal is inferred from valid PCM samples. I²S cannot electrically identify the microphone; a connected but silent module may show no signal.

01.title: Change RGB brightness
01.try: Change BRIGHTNESS from 40 to 15, download the sketch and upload it from Arduino IDE. Disconnect the serial monitor first.
01.expect: The rainbow continues at a lower brightness. The monitor displays chip information.

02.title: Compare two speeds
02.try: With the sketch uploaded and the terminal connected, send blink 200, then blink 800. Read how command() handles the text.
02.expect: The LED changes from fast to slow blinking; the monitor confirms each mode.

P1.title: Test the BOOT input
P1.try: Change the pressed interval from 100 to 50 ms, upload the sketch, then hold BOOT.
P1.expect: The user LED blinks faster while BOOT is held; the monitor reports the button state.

P2.title: Mix a colour, then dim it
P2.try: Upload the sketch, connect the console and send rgb 255 80 0. Compare level 20 with level 100.
P2.expect: The LED stays orange while its brightness changes; off turns it dark.

P3.title: Compare raw and calibrated readings
P3.try: Move the potentiometer near its midpoint and locate both ADC reads in the sketch.
P3.expect: The monitor reports a raw count and a millivolt value for the same position.

P4.title: Count the on-board devices
P4.try: Run the scanner and compare its addresses with the five expected sensors in the guide.
P4.expect: The serial monitor lists the addresses that answered on the board's I²C bus.

P5.title: Check that a file survives reset
P5.try: Run the sketch with a FAT32 microSD card, then press RST twice and read the log again.
P5.expect: Each boot appends one more line to /pulsar.txt without deleting earlier lines.

P6.title: Test the UART loopback
P6.try: Join TX0 to RX0, upload the sketch and send hello UART. Then remove the jumper and send it again.
P6.expect: The first message returns as loopback: hello UART; the second no longer returns.

D1.title: Prove it is a BMI270
D1.try: Plug the BMI270 into QWIIC, upload the sketch and open the monitor.
D1.expect: The monitor lists found 0x68 (or 0x69), then chip ID 0x24 (BMI270).

D2.title: See how the light graph is built
D2.try: Find DevLabDDP::Master in the sketch, then follow the ADC reading into drawGraph().
D2.expect: The OLED plots the last 126 samples while the serial monitor prints raw values.

D3.title: Watch the filter work
D3.try: Wire the TMP235 to A2, upload the sketch and open the Serial Plotter.
D3.expect: Around 750 mV and 25 °C at room temperature; pinch the sensor and the filtered line rises smoothly.

O1.title: Turn on the OLED
O1.try: Upload o1-oled.ino with only the SSD1306 connected to QWIIC.
O1.expect: The screen shows Pulsar C5 and OLED ready.

I1.title: Post to ThingSpeak
I1.try: Fill in WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASS and THINGSPEAK_API_KEY, upload the sketch and open the monitor.
I1.expect: The monitor shows the IP, channel and band, then a reading with HTTP 200 every 20 seconds.

I2.title: Notify the phone
I2.try: Upload the sketch, connect to PulsarC5-BLE from nRF Connect, subscribe and touch the pad.
I2.expect: The phone receives touched and released, and the monitor prints the same.

00.title: Check the REPL
00.try: After installing the firmware, connect the serial port at 115200 baud and send the test command.
00.expect: The console displays MicroPython OK and returns to the >>> prompt. The first .py file appears in lesson 01.

01.title: Change RGB brightness
01.try: Change BRIGHTNESS from 40 to 15 and press Run on board. Press Stop before editing again.
01.expect: The LED cycles through the same colours at a lower brightness.

02.title: Change the LED timing
02.try: Change sleep_ms(12) to sleep_ms(30) and run the file again.
02.expect: The external LED fades up and down more slowly.

P1.title: Test the BOOT input
P1.try: Run gpio.py, then change the pressed interval from 100 to 50 ms and hold BOOT.
P1.expect: The user LED blinks faster while BOOT is held; the REPL reports its state.

P2.title: Mix a colour, then dim it
P2.try: Run rgb_mixer.py, then send rgb 255 80 0, level 20 and level 100 in the terminal.
P2.expect: The LED stays orange while its brightness changes; off turns it dark.

P3.title: Compare ADC and voltage
P3.try: Run adc.py and turn the potentiometer while comparing read_u16() with read_uv().
P3.expect: The 16-bit scaled value and approximate millivolts follow the knob.

P4.title: Find the on-board sensors
P4.try: Run i2c_scan.py and compare the reported addresses with the five devices in the guide.
P4.expect: The REPL lists the devices that answered on GPIO2/GPIO3.

P5.title: Check that the file keeps its data
P5.try: Install sdcard.py on the board, insert a FAT32 card, then run microsd.py twice and read /sd/pulsar.txt after each run.
P5.expect: Each run appends a line without deleting the earlier one.

P6.title: Test the UART loopback
P6.try: Bridge A2/GPIO4 to A3/GPIO5, run uart_loopback.py and send hello UART in the terminal.
P6.expect: The script prints loopback: hello UART; without the jumper it reports no response.

D1.title: Identify and move the BMI270
D1.try: Run bmi270_id.py; then install bmi270.py and run bmi270_motion.py.
D1.expect: The terminal confirms chip ID 0x24 and shows acceleration and gyroscope readings on all three axes.

D2.title: Plot light on the OLED
D2.try: Install ssd1306.py, run oled_light.py, then cover and illuminate the TEMT6000.
D2.expect: The terminal identifies device 0x0102 and the OLED graph follows the light.

D3.title: Watch the filter work
D3.try: Wire the TMP235 to A2 and run tmp235_temperature.py.
D3.expect: Around 750 mV and 25 °C at room temperature; pinch the sensor and the filtered column rises smoothly.

O1.title: Turn on the OLED
O1.try: Install ssd1306.py, then run oled.py with only the display connected.
O1.expect: The screen shows Pulsar C5 and MicroPython.

I1.title: Post to ThingSpeak
I1.try: Fill in WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASS and THINGSPEAK_API_KEY in thingspeak_dht.py and run it.
I1.expect: The terminal shows the IP, channel and band, then a reading with HTTP 200 every 20 seconds.

I2.title: Notify the phone
I2.try: Run ble_touch.py, connect to PulsarC5-BLE from nRF Connect, subscribe and touch the pad.
I2.expect: The phone and the terminal show touched and released; Stop switches the radio off.

adc.title: ADC channels on the header

states.qwiic: Only if nothing is on QWIIC

adc.note: The ESP32-C5 has one 12-bit ADC (ADC1) with six channels, on GPIO1–GPIO6. It keeps working while Wi-Fi is on. SDA and SCL already carry the on-board sensors and their 4.7 kΩ pull-ups, so their readings are not usable.
adc.drawn: Each ADC1 channel is boxed beside its pad.

avoidWhy.strapping: Strapping pin: the chip reads its level at reset to choose how it boots. You can use it, but avoid strong pull-ups or pull-downs and don't hold it high or low while the board restarts.
avoidWhy.usb: Native USB data line (D−/D+): the serial console and flashing go through it. Using it for something else cuts the USB connection.
avoidWhy.uart: UART0, the boot serial console. Use it only if you don't need that console.
avoidWhy.control: A board control pin, not a GPIO: pulling it to GND switches the chip off or resets it.

explorer.choose: Select a pin to see its details.
explorer.qwiic: Qwiic uses SDA on GPIO1 and SCL on GPIO6. These differ from the SDA/SCL header pads, which use GPIO2/GPIO3.

pulsar.note: Documented map for revision V1.2.3. D2/RGB is GPIO0, the data line of the on-board RGB LED.
pulsar.strapping: GPIO 2, 3, 7, 25, 26, 27 and 28 are strapping pins: keep them free of strong pull-ups or pull-downs at reset.
